examples.text: Девушка, я не собираюсь с вами ссориться.
examples.trans: Miss, I have no intention of quarreling with you.

examples.text: Вы куда смотрите? Сперва соль, потом вино!
examples.trans: Where are you looking? First salt, then wine!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'fall', paired with 'упасть'.

examples.text: Падайте на колени, молите о пощаде.
examples.trans: Fall to your knees, beg for mercy.

examples.text: Итак, я аккуратно попадаю под колёса.
examples.trans: So, I carefully get under the wheels.

examples.text: Купят джипов, не поймёшь, под какой падать.
examples.trans: They buy all these SUVs, you can't tell which one to fall under.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Если женщина, жди неприятностей и не жди чаевых.
examples.trans: If it is a woman, expect trouble and don't expect tips.

examples.text: У вас написано, что вы открываетесь в одиннадцать.
examples.trans: Your sign says that you open at eleven.

examples.text: У вас, наверное, часы спешат.
examples.trans: Your watch is probably running fast.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'knees' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Падайте на колени, молите о пощаде.
examples.trans: Fall to your knees, beg for mercy.

examples.text: Я стою на коленях.
examples.trans: I'm on my knees.

examples.text: У меня болит колено.
examples.trans: My knee hurts.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'beg, implore'.

examples.text: Падайте на колени, молите о пощаде.
examples.trans: Fall to your knees, beg for mercy.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и молить вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and beg on time.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'about', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спортсмены — самые суеверные люди в мире?
examples.trans: Are athletes the most superstitious people in the world?

examples.text: Ничего подобного. Самые суеверные люди — официанты.
examples.trans: Nothing of the sort. The most superstitious people are waiters.

examples.text: Соль просыпала. Ничего страшного.
examples.trans: I spilled the salt. No big deal.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'щада'). Common feminine noun meaning 'mercy' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Падайте на колени, молите о пощаде.
examples.trans: Fall to your knees, beg for mercy.

examples.text: На кухне ресторана всегда есть пощада.
examples.trans: In the restaurant kitchen there is always mercy.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'otherwise', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Если женщина, жди неприятностей и не жди чаевых.
examples.trans: If it is a woman, expect trouble and don't expect tips.

examples.text: Иначе уволю обоих!
examples.trans: Otherwise I will fire both of you!

examples.text: Екатерина, зайдите ко мне.
examples.trans: Yekaterina, come into my office.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'волить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'will fire', paired with 'увольнять'.

examples.text: Ты уволен!
examples.trans: You're fired!

examples.text: Его уволили.
examples.trans: He was fired.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'both', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Можете искать новую работу. Оба!
examples.trans: You can look for a new job. Both of you!

examples.text: А что эта особа здесь делает?
examples.trans: And what is this person doing here?

examples.text: Вы сейчас отсюда оба уходите.
examples.trans: You both leave here right now.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to cry', paired with 'заплакать'.

examples.text: Плакать буду, но уволю.
examples.trans: I will cry, but I will fire you.

examples.text: Ну не плачь ты.
examples.trans: Please don't cry.

examples.text: Почему девочка плачет?
examples.trans: Why is the little girl crying?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ничего подобного. Самые суеверные люди — официанты.
examples.trans: Nothing of the sort. The most superstitious people are waiters.

examples.text: Соль просыпала. Ничего страшного.
examples.trans: I spilled the salt. No big deal.

examples.text: Как это ничего страшного?
examples.trans: What do you mean, no big deal?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'but, after all', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я же говорила, что поссоримся.
examples.trans: I told you we would quarrel.

examples.text: Если женщина, жди неприятностей и не жди чаевых.
examples.trans: If it is a woman, expect trouble and don't expect tips.

examples.text: Вы тоже не совсем москвичка.
examples.trans: You are not quite a Muscovite yourself either.
